HEADLINE: Tax cut 'will boost customer service'
TEXT:
Mark Steinert, the head of Australia's largest residential developer Stockland, says companies would use a corporate tax cut to invest in customer service as they strove to become more competitive.

Mr Steinert said one benefit of the government's plan to cut the corporate tax rate to 25 per cent from the current 30 per cent would be to give companies that have cut costs sharply in recent years a chance to put money back into their businesses.

"We've have had a long period of cost-cutting," Mr Steinert told The Australian Financial Review after reporting earnings last week. "... what we're seeing more and more is people are recognising the real value, in this disrupted economic environment we live in, of the value of customer service."

The opportunity for Australia was not to compete on cost, but service, Mr Steinert said.

"In our relatively wealthy society, people are willing to pay for differentiated service."

The Stockland boss, who reiterated commitments by other company heads that tax cuts would not simply flow into shareholders' pockets, said the lower tax rate was necessary to keep Australia competitive with the rest of the world.

"We live in a global capital market," he said. "To the extent corporate leaders and chairmen and boards are saying to the extent we have a lower tax expense, we're willing to direct the savings to increase employment and wages, that's positive to the broader economy. It would be a real plus for the longer-term growth cycle." He was supported by Scentre Group chief executive Peter Allen, who said a cut would boost Australia's overall tax intake as employment grew.

"I strongly believe that in improving and being competitive - Australia needs to be competitive in the world environment - and that therefore tax is a big impost for all companies, so to be in a competitive environment, if we are competitive, then that allows companies to attract the best people to be able to grow their businesses and that will flow through in terms of greater employment," Mr Allen also told the Financial Review after reporting earnings.

Earlier this week, family entertainment business and Dreamworld owner Ardent Leisure, which makes 80 per cent of its revenue from its US-based Main Event Entertainment division, on Monday booked a $14.9 million deferred tax benefit from President Donald Trump's reforms that cut the US corporate tax rate to 21 per cent from 35 per cent.

Chairman Gary Weiss declined to comment on the Australian corporate tax debate.

"Over time even a lower tax rate will probably increase the tax take," he said.

Companies that had more cash to hand would pay more to compete for staff, GPT chief executive Bob Johnston said earlier this month. "It just puts more money into the system," Mr Johnston said. "From that, if there is more competition for those employees you'll probably see a bit of wages growth ... We are seeing other parts of the world with a much more competitive tax framework than Australia."

Over time even a lower tax rate will probably increase the tax take. Gary Weiss, Ardent

HEADLINE: Low-grade malls to 'struggle' amid retail change: Brookes
TEXT:
Veteran executive and former Myer boss Bernie Brookes has warned some lower-grade shopping centres will struggle to remain viable as pressure mounts in the retail sector.

Mr Brookes is fresh from a 30-month stint in South Africa where he led its largest non-food retailer, Edcon.

The former Myer chief executive is back in Australia in time to see the company he once led in turmoil and shopping centres around the country facing headwinds from e-commerce and softening consumer sentiment.

"The big successful shopping centres - the Chadstones, the Bondis, potentially the Eastlands - those shopping centres have a good future because they are A-grade shopping centres," Mr Brookes told ABC Radio yesterday.

"Potentially, the fallout is going to be in the B and C-class malls, the second and third-rate malls who are going to struggle to get tenants.

"Every retail store in Australia is talking about reducing the number of stores, they are all talking about the size of stores," Mr Brookes said.

"The implication of that for shopping centres is quite significant. Going forward, you can see a lot of them struggling to get tenants, to get shopping centres full."

The past year or more has been a busy one for major retail landlords such as Scentre, which owns Westfield malls, Vicinity Centres which partly owns Chadstone in Melbourne, and diversified players GPT, Mirvac and Stockland, which have malls in their portfolios.

There has been considerable activity in the portfolios of the major owners in an effort to bolster their assets in a sector that has already experienced a wave of retail administrations.

Reprising a theme espoused by analysts and landlords, Mr Brookes said major malls such as Chadstone, which is partly owned by billionaire John Gandel, would remain successful because they represented a "great day out" as destinations in themselves.

"But ... some of the second and third-rate malls are going to struggle as retailers consolidate," he said.

That analysis also applied to department stores, such as Myer, and discount department stores that have been too slow to revamp their offering with better service and a more attractive experience of shopping.

HEADLINE: AusPost won't rule out site sales
TEXT:
Australia Post chief executive Christine Holgate has left the door open for further landmark sales from the national carrier's $1.6 billion portfolio.

Last year's sale of the freehold of the Sydney GPO to Singapore's Far East Organisation and its sister company Sino Land Company helped underpin AusPost's $217 million half-year profit for 2018.

Without the one-off boost, AusPost's underlying earnings were only just marginally profitable, placing additional pressure on it to dip into its enviable property portfolio to prop up future results.

"We are holding back on property sales at the moment," Ms Holgate told The Australian Financial Review.

"In the future we may need to do some ... but we would like to focus on growing the business sustainably."

AusPost's portfolio of land and buildings had a gross book value of $1.6 billion at June 30 last year.

Taking into account accumulated depreciation, the portfolio was ascribed a net value of $825.1 million.

It is a diverse portfolio of post offices, mail and parcel processing facilities among other delivery infrastructure across the country.

That includes some of the country's most historic and nationally significant buildings, the group of stunning, colonial-era GPOs that have been at the heart of city life across Australia's capitals.

Ms Holgate's predecessor, Ahmed Fahour, oversaw an ambitious plan in 2016 to sell down those historic buildings, the crown jewels of the portfolio, into a fund run by Eureka Funds Management.

The complex proposal was eventually abandoned although a single freehold asset, Sydney's GPO building at 1 Martin Place, was ultimately sold for $150 million to its major tenants, Far East and Sino Land which had a 99-year lease on the site and own the Westin Hotel next door.

"It is critically important that we return Australia Post to sustainable growth and not allow our viability to be so dependent on property asset sales," an Australia Post spokesman said yesterday.

The national postal service has been previously adroit in leveraging uplift from its property portfolio.

The large site of an Australia Post mail centre on Spencer Street in Melbourne's CBD was progressively developed into two major police facilities by Cbus Property.

AusPost had retained a stake in half of the large site that was still being developed and last year sold its half stake for $347.8 million.

HEADLINE: Security fears based on 'groundless suspicions', says Huawei chief
TEXT:
In rare public commentary, Huawei's global chief executive Ken Hu has dismissed any suggestion the Chinese telecommunications giant is a security risk, saying US and Australian concerns are based on "groundless suspicions" and unfair to the company.

"We welcome discussions and even debate if it is based on facts," he said. "If it is based on groundless suspicions, it is not a constructive way to resolve the issue."

Mr Hu was responding to revelations in The Australian Financial Review that the US had warned the Australian government to exclude Huawei from the imminent deployment of the new super-fast 5G mobile network due to security concerns.

The Australian government has now ordered a full national security assessment of Huawei's involvement from the newly established critical infrastructure centre in the Department of Home Affairs.

This is even though Huawei is already conducting 5G trials for the major telecommunications companies in Australia and is on the government's 5G working group.

"We are very happy to conduct open and transparent discussions with the Australian government and telecom operators," Mr Hu told the Financial Review while attending the World Mobile Congress in Barcelona. For the past 30 years we have been providing products and services for telecom operators and we have maintained a very strong record of security.

"We are making relentless efforts in technological innovation and we are placing technology security as one of our top priorities. It would not be fair for us if all of our 30 years of a strong track record on security are disregarded based on groundless suspicions."

He described Huawei as "very sorry" the words and concerns expressed were not based on solid facts.

But the company headquarters is privately deeply alarmed about the prospect of a re-run of the National Broadband Network shock when Huawei was abruptly banned from any involvement in the project by the Abbott government.

This also came after security warnings from the US and was deeply embarrassing to the Chinese company, particularly given its global ambitions.

But since then Huawei has grown spectacularly to become the world's biggest supplier of telco equipment and the third largest mobile phone supplier with revenues of $US92 billion last year. This is despite being effectively blocked from much of the US market.

Huawei is one of the biggest industry exhibitors at the big annual gathering of telco suppliers and operators in Barcelona with Mr Hu describing 5G as "the hot issue" this year.

In the wake of the NBN ban, Huawei in Australia has also tried to alleviate any security concerns by holding regular discussions in Canberra, including security agencies - as they do with many other governments and telecom operators, particularly in Europe and Canada.

The Shenzhen headquarters of Huawei still considers Australia, along with the US and Taiwan, as one of only three countries that are "hostile" to the company. Some members of the US Congress are suggesting Huawei's presence in countries with close security ties to the US could make its own telecommunications networks more vulnerable.

But any move to block Huawei from 5G would mean Australia's approach to the development of the network and network security contrasts with that of governments in the rest of the world bar the US.

According to Mr Hu, Huawei now has memorandums of understandings on 5G with 45 different telcos and is conducting pre-commercial 5G trials in major cities including Seoul, Tokyo, London, Milan and Vancouver.

He pointed out the entire industry now revolves around global supply and value chains, meaning many leading ICT companies use components that are made in China no matter where they are headquartered. "The view that a company headquartered in China cannot be trusted is problematic," he said. "For any new technology, including 5G, when it is introduced into the market, security is one factor all stakeholders will consider.

"Huawei is one of the leading players in the 5G technological development so we are thinking about ensuring security and providing the highest level of security protection when we work on standards and technological development in co-operation with telcos and governments."

Huawei had had a successful experience with 4G in Australia, he said, where the company has been the key supplier for Vodafone and Optus. It will also supply the equipment to TPG for its new mobile network.

Telstra retains Huawei's competitor, Ericsson, as its major equipment supplier for the rollout of 5G.

Andy Penn, Telstra's chief executive and another Barcelona attendee, said he would not comment on Telstra's trialling of any other particular vendors because of commercial sensitivities. But Penn still told the Financial Review that "you can imagine we would be investigating all of the best technology that is available", indicating Huawei is also doing some trials for Telstra on 5G.

Ironically, one of Huawei's latest and most popular mobile phones, the Mate 10 Pro, was named after the Australian concept of mateship.

This is the same phone that Verizon and AT&T have now dropped plans to sell following pressure from Congress although it is available from other smaller telco players.

The still emerging technology of 5G is designed to greatly improve speed, efficiency and capacity of the mobile network. This will also help accelerate the growth of the "internet of things" where objects are connected to one another via sensors, backed by increasing automation of the network and, over time, the increased use of artificial intelligence to differentiate parts of the network.

There are different views on whether this makes 5G less or more secure to any potential hacking given the ever more sophisticated technology to counter any potential intrusions and the obvious commercial need to protect the reputations of global equipment suppliers in terms of providing maximum security.

Penn said that security was obviously a critical aspect of Telstra's network planning.

"The point about the internet of things is the more entry points you have into effectively the core of someone's network, clearly you are opening up a bigger perimeter. The more things that are connected, the more ways in there are," he said.

"The reason security is talked a lot about in relation to the internet of things is that where you have millions of connected devices, all of a sudden you can hack in via a very innocuous device in the home. If you increase the perimeter and increase the number of things that are connected, you need to increase the security or make sure the security on those things is commensurate because every one of them is a point of entry into a network."

Jennifer Hewett is attending the Mobile World Congress as a guest of Huawei.

HEADLINE: Macquarie confident its acquisition of UK bank will help it turn green to gold
TEXT:
When the UK government wanted to sell its Green Investment Bank, it was obvious Macquarie Group would be the natural owner.

Green Investment Bank, which had a track record of building renewable infrastructure assets, fitted naturally with Macquarie's combination of skills including distribution of international equity, debt financing and funds asset management. A Macquarie-led consortium went ahead with the £2.3 billion purchase in August last year.

GIB is a potential game-changer for Macquarie globally because the assets, skills and connections it brings to the group will give it an edge in the two investment mega-trends of renewable energy and impact investing.

The Green Investment Group, as is it now known, set up the world's first offshore wind infrastructure fund. Macquarie has significant ownership stakes in 48 per cent of offshore wind assets in Britain, including the Gwynt y Mor offshore wind farm in Wales, the largest in the UK.

David Fass, head of Macquarie Group's European operations, says billions in renewable energy deals will flow through Macquarie entities over the next decade. "The firm has a very high profile obviously in Australia and with the maturity and the types of transactions that we've done over the last 10 years here in the UK, and in Germany, in particular, we now have a high-ish profile here too," he says. Features p40

HEADLINE: EY partner in sex harassment claims
TEXT:
Ernst & Young's South Australian managing partner has been suspended amid allegations of sexual harassment by a junior female staff member, sparking a CEO warning to the firm's 540 partners over workplace behaviour.

Don Manifold has been Adelaide office managing partner at the big-four accounting and consulting firm since 2015. He was suspended on January 19 after the sexual harassment allegations were made by the female staffer.

The woman was suspended almost a month earlier after allegations of inappropriate behaviour were made against her.

She could not be reached for comment. Mr Manifold has denied any wrongdoing and declined to comment.

In an email sent to the firm's partners, EY Oceania chief executive Tony Johnson said last night: "Recently, I was made aware of allegations of inappropriate conduct, involving a partner and a staff member of the firm.

"As soon as the allegations became known, both parties were suspended from the office, with a presumption of innocence, whilst an investigation of claims and counter-claims is being undertaken. These breaches will be taken seriously and commensurate ramifications will be determined, actioned and remain confidential."

HEADLINE: Cormann defends rail investment
TEXT:
Finance Minister Mathias Cormann insists the Coalition's $10 billion inland rail is a legitimate off-budget investment because it elevates the capital value of the government company building the tracks and provides a future treasurer with a sellable asset.

Even if the Melbourne-to-Brisbane Inland Rail doesn't generate enough revenue to directly cover its capital costs, Senator Cormann said its accounting and budget treatment was appropriate under the Charter of Budget Honesty.

He strongly rejected suggestions it would be at risk of rebounding on the federal budget should it go bad.

Senator Cormann made the remarks in response to questions in estimates yesterday from Labor senator Kimberley Kitching after the Australian Rail Track Corporation chief executive, John Fullerton, revealed last week that from "a strict ARTC point of view, no, the revenues that flow to us wouldn't cover the full capital cost and provide a return".

Governments are increasingly opting for so-called "equity funding" as an alternative to traditional grant payments to states for transport projects because they aren't treated as straight Commonwealth spending and thereby do not add to net debt levels.

Another example is the controversial budget treatment of the NBN Co, which this month admitted that changes in its pricing model will mean it will miss its 2021 revenue targets, reigniting debate over whether the project should be brought onto the budget to enable reductions in wholesale pricing.

In justifying the Inland Rail equity investment, Senator Cormann indicated the Commonwealth was focused on ARTC's total returns and dividends, its capital value, and its potential prospects as a sellable asset. "In terms of the expectation of whether or not there is a positive return, it is not only a matter of the cash flows, that is the revenues," Senator Cormann said.

"It is also a matter of the impact of the expected future capital value, the expected future sales value.

"That is something the Labor Party should be well aware of because that is the basis on which you in government ... classified the investment in NBN as an equity injection. We expect the ARTC to continue to deliver a positive rate of return to the Commonwealth."

HEADLINE: Unis told to lift productivity ahead of face-off with minister
TEXT:
A professor of management at Melbourne University says unis have paid only lip service towards lifting their productivity. His comment comes as the federal Education Minister and the universities go head to head at a conference in Canberra today on the future of the higher education sector.

Professor Danny Samson says universities should be able to raise the productivity of their physical assets.

He says the traditional teaching year is only 24 weeks long, which means as many as 10,000 tutorial rooms and 100 lecture halls around the country are used for only half their working lives.

If unis switched to a trimester system and extended teaching times, there could be a 50 per cent gain in productivity and the opportunity cost to students would be reduced as the time to complete degrees would be sliced by up to a third.

Professor Samson says uni enterprise bargaining agreements should be overhauled to remove the obligation to give all staff research time.

Most universities work with a 40/40/20 system, which means all academics are allowed to do research for 40 per cent of their time, teach for 40 per cent and do administration work for the other 20 per cent.

"In many other industries people specialise in what they are best at. But we expect everybody to be a competent and active researcher, teacher and engaged with admin.

"I'm doing a lot of work with Toyota. They don't expect people to be good at everything. In higher education we've got people who are fantastic researchers but not so good at teaching. We could increase our research productivity and teaching effectiveness - if we redesigned our EBAs."

Higher education consultant Andrew Dempster, from Proofpoint Advisory, says most universities want to be more agile but it's hard because they are crushed by bureaucracy, which is partly of their own making.

"It's not uncommon to see university change initiatives grind to a halt as a result of lengthy internal debate followed by several trips to the Fair Work Commission," he said.

He says simplifying industrial awards would make a huge difference, although a recent trade-off of paying 17 per cent superannuation for all non-union staff in exchange for a simplified IR arrangement had added to long-term costs - just as the government was giving them a squeeze.

The federal Education Minister, Simon Birmingham, will attempt to placate universities today, promising to overhaul the highly-criticised system of academic accreditation.

But the unis are elevating their criticism of the freeze on funding for new students, saying there is a high risk to social cohesion by denying a university education to tens of thousands of Australians.

The minister and the unis have been in open conflict since $2.2 billion in funding was sliced off the higher education sector in December.

Senator Birmingham will tell vice-chancellors he's adopting a report that has made scathing criticism of the way universities and teachers are accredited.

The report, commissioned by the Higher Education Standards Panel, says accreditation is idiosyncratic, excessive and makes unreasonable demands.

There are as many as 100 accreditation bodies covering professions represented in education and on top of that unis have to meet requirements laid down by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Teqsa).

The minister will tell the vice-chancellors he wants to limit professional accreditation and avoid duplication with Teqsa.

Universities are tackling the minister by appealing to the public and business for a reversal of the funding cuts.

HEADLINE: Coal push could kill off Snowy 2.0
TEXT:
Snowy Hydro is yet to model the impact of the National Energy Guarantee on the Snowy 2.0 expansion but a top executive has warned the construction of new coal-fired power stations would jeopardise the project's viability.

The taxpayer-owned company's chief operating officer Roger Whitby also told a Senate estimates hearing yesterday that higher renewable energy targets would benefit Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's pet pumped-hydro project.

The Turnbull government is attempting to end the so-called climate wars while tackling higher power prices for consumers and businesses and boosting reliability of power through its National Energy Guarantee, or NEG, which will impose dispatchable capacity and emissions reductions on electricity retailers.

Mr Whitby told senators the feasibility study into Snowy 2.0 had been completed before details of the NEG were known but would be updated once the final design was settled.

He believed a "well-designed NEG should enhance the viability of Snowy 2.0 project but we are not assuming it in terms of the work that has been done."

"The two elements of the NEG, the reliability or dispatchability arm and the emissions reduction arm, both those elements complement Snowy Hydro's operations generally. They are both value-enhancing elements for our business."

Mr Whitby said Snowy 2.0 was a "project for the future", not the current state of the energy market.

Asked by NSW Labor Senator Kristina Keneally whether construction of the new coal-fired power stations to boost baseload power, as some Coalition MPs have called for, would undermine the business case for Snowy 2.0, Mr Whitby replied: "Simply put, yes".

"Assuming the world most players accept where coal-fired generation is ageing and retiring and there is increasing penetration of intermittent renewable energy, clearly if we have a reversion essentially to the past, then of course under that scenario Snowy 2 is not viable," he said. "Why this project wasn't done in the past - in fact some of the early visions for this project were floated in 1966 - in that time new coal-fired plants were being added and without imposts or constraints on carbon dioxide production, coal-fired generation in that time was the most economically viable way to provide electricity."

Mr Whitby agreed with Greens Senator Janet Rice that an increase to the renewable energy target would benefit Snowy Hydro.

"I think the more that intermittent renewables enter the market over time, the more and more need there will be for storage projects in general, whether it be Snowy 2 or Snowy 3 or alternate [projects]," he said.

Mr Whitby said the estimated cost of $3.8 billion to $4.5 billion to build Snowy 2.0 proposed in the feasibility study released in December remained valid. He said the project had a finish date of 2024, and concluded Snowy Hydro Ltd would be able to fund the project itself from its cash flow and taking on debt.

Mr Whitby said significant work was still under way on geotechnical studies, detailed design work and a tender process, with a final investment decision to be made on whether Snowy 2.0 goes ahead to be completed before the end of 2018.

The Commonwealth owns 13 per cent of Snowy Hydro Ltd, with negotiations under way to acquire NSW's (58 per cent) and Victoria's (29 per cent) shares.

While some conservative MPs flagged concerns over the design of the NEG earlier this year, Environment and Energy Minister Josh Frydenberg told the Coalition party room yesterday he hoped to finalise an agreement with the states by the middle of the year, with South Australia's Labor government the only one standing in the way.

HEADLINE: 'Vulnerable': Australia Post warns of losses
TEXT:
Australia Post has delivered a $217 million half-year profit, boosted by the $150 million sale of the Sydney GPO, Christmas parcel sales and the same-sex marriage survey.

But new chief executive Christine Holgate has warned the government that the profit is vulnerable, and change and transformation was urgently needs.

Revenue increased by 3 per cent to $3.6 billion, but the 8 per cent increase in parcel volumes could not mask the 10 per cent fall in addressed letter volumes, which "would have experienced an even sharper decline" save for the Australian Marriage Law Postal Survey, which created a $26.3 million revenue surge last year.

Ms Holgate said while half-year profit was up 65 per cent, based on underlying earnings it was "only just marginally profitable" with "no low hanging fruit" after cutting $113 million in expenses. It expected to make a loss in the second half.

Post's operating earnings grew just 1 per cent, delivering a slim dividend to the government of $33 million.

"If you strip out the unusual or one-off items, profit has declined but we remain profitable," Ms Holgate told a Parliamentary committee yesterday.

"When faced with such significant disruption and change, it makes it a vulnerable result. We need to work with the government to find a viable future."

Ms Holgate emphasised the importance of her Asia strategy, with inbound parcel volumes up 45 per cent and almost all coming from China. However, she admitted the growth is yet to convert into profits and Post had only a small part of the outbound parcel market, where it faces tough competition from international rivals.

"We have a successful parcel business ... but it operates in a competitive market against large foreign-owned entities," she told the committee in her first appearance before the Senate's environment and communications committee alongside Communications Minister Mitch Fifield.

One-off property transactions and revaluations added $44 million to the bottom line, after the business controversially sold Sydney's historic GPO in Martin Place to Singaporean billionaire developers Robert and Phillip Ng for a reported $150 million last March.

"We are holding back on property sales at the moment," Ms Holgate told the Financial Review. "In the future we may need to do some ... but we would like to focus on growing the business sustainably." Ms Holgate said there was an opportunity to "reform our LPO network" and examine Post's business two-speed mail.

Australia Post executives were also grilled by the parliamentary committee about the failed Digital Mailbox, which was closed last year after costing $23 million in 2015-16 alone.

Ms Holgate, who took two weeks off before she started as CEO to travel to Bhutan to help out at a Buddhist temple in the high mountains, has been busy meeting stakeholders including the unions since she started in her role.

The British-born CEO surprised staff when she turned up at the Melbourne Gateway processing facility just before Christmas with her mum and a Buddhist monk to bless the building and workers.

"People kept stopping me to ask about my work in Bhutan and when I told them the Buddhist monk was coming to Australia, they made me promise to bring him," she said. "I am not Buddhist but it's important to recognise everyone in the workplace and make them feel welcome."

Ms Holgate last month announced a dramatic shake-up of the company, with half a dozen senior executives, including chief customer officer Christine Corbett, losing out following a strategic review by PwC to refocus on customers and Asia.
